There's so many things one can do to make it so that a stray hold person spell is not enough to outright win the fight.

For one, Hold Person allows another save each round, which means that you need a very long unlucky streak not to break free, ever, secondly you can have things like spell resistance, damage reduction or elemental resistances to make sure that you can do without the moment of respite, but having it won't allow you an immediate win.

Basically when it comes to designing encounters that aren't too easy but also are not too hard to win, it's all about attrition.

The boss can't stomp the whole party in two attacks, but needs to be tanky enough not to get buttfucked in 3 rounds. Either scenarios leave the scenario in the hands of the dice, which you definitely don't want. It should be about playing smart and taking the right risks.

For instance, one encounter I built centuries ago went something like this:

The boss was a kind of queen bee type thing. Attacking it released swarms of smaller enemies that had a fairly weak poison (DC 12), but attacked in a swarm, leading to fairly high attack bonus. The swarms were not particularly dangerous on their own, dealing 1d4 damage to a party that was very able to take it, but if they became too many the sheer amount of attacks and rolls to prevent poison would've eventually led to the party failing rolls and starting to lose Str points (1d4 per poisoning) en masse, which are a lot fewer than hit points even at higher levels.

The players had met those swarms previously during the adventure and had learned to counter them with a certain degree of efficacy, so I basically built the encounter around them pulling all the stops and increasing their efficiency in dealing with them to the max while also attacking the main monster.

By the end we had 2 or 3 members of the party running around with torches, wands of burning hands and similar aoe clearing, and people chugging remove poison, protection from poison and so on while the barbarian was chopping the queen bee to pieces with his axe and providing more targets.

Holding the queen bee would've just prevented the one attack a turn, and not that great an attack either.

There's way to build around a party's skillset without nullifying it, it's just a matter of having a DM who knows how to build one.

I've encouraged my DM to build more complex and/or more frequent encounters, which has helped substantially to cut down on one-mob facerolls. And swarms of bees...we don't speak of dire bees. They're unkind to wizards.
